text:
You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.3. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.3.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.3 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 18 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
This is a public goods game — each token I keep in my own account gives me 1 point but costs each of the other 3 players 0.3 points, a total externality of -0.9. Each token I put in the group account only pays me 0.3 points and doesn't seem to affect the others directly, based on the wording that group account tokens pay me specifically.

Working out the totals: a private token yields +0.1 net socially (1 to me minus 0.9 to others), while a group token yields +0.3 net socially to me alone. So contributing to the group is actually more socially efficient, but individually, keeping tokens private still dominates since 1 point beats 0.3 point regardless of what others do. That's the core dilemma — the dominant individual strategy is to keep everything private, even though group contribution produces more total value.

Since this repeats over 10 rounds with unknown opponents, I'm considering whether to open with cooperation (full group contribution) as a signal and adjust based on outcomes, versus playing the individually rational all-private strategy from the start. I think I'll lean toward contributing to the group in round one to test for reciprocity, while recognizing the math slightly favors defection if others don't cooperate back.

Redoing the math properly: if others keep all private, that's 18 points lost regardless of my choice. Contributing to group gives me -12, keeping private gives me 2 — a 14-point swing favoring private. So the dominant strategy is clearly to keep tokens private; cooperation only pays off if enough others reciprocate.

Running the full numbers, if everyone keeps all tokens each player ends up with 20 points, but if everyone contributes fully to the group each gets 42 points—so cooperation is far more socially efficient even though keeping tokens is the individually dominant strategy. With 10 repeated rounds rather than a single shot, I'm weighing whether to lean toward cooperation despite the short-term incentive to defect.

Still, opening with full cooperation is a reasonable strategy to signal intent and test reciprocity in a repeated game, so I'll start by contributing all 20 tokens and adjust based on how others respond.
